newsitem.title: SAUDI ARABIA: Saudi king committed to protect U.S. troops - Perry.
newsitem.headline: Saudi king committed to protect U.S. troops - Perry.

text.p: Saudi Arabia's King Fahd on Saturday gave his commitment to further increases in protection and living conditions for 5,700 U.S. troops in the kingdom in a plan that is costing $300 million, U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry said.

Perry held talks with King Fahd in Riyadh and then flew to this remote, heavily protected Saudi desert base where 4,000 American airmen and a number of warplanes have been moved in the last two months to protect them from possible attacks in the wake of two bombings since November last year.

"We got the king's very strong commitment to continue providing support as we go into phase two" of current work to upgrade facilities at Sultan and at Eskan village near Riyadh, another highly secure facility where 1,700 American troops are now being moved, Perry said.

The forces have been consolidated at the two facilities after bombing attacks in Riyadh in November last year and in Dhahran on June 25 that killed a total of 24 U.S. troops. The airbase is at al-Kharj, 60 miles (100 km) southeast of Riyadh.
Perry told reporters flying with him later to the United Arab Emirates that the security moves had so far cost Washington about $150 million.
He said Saudi Arabia was likely to spend the same amount on further upgrades, including better housing.
After a brief stop in Abu Dhabi where he was expected to meet UAE President Sheikh Zaid bin Sultan al-Nahayan, Perry was to head to Tokyo on the final leg of a global tour.

The secretary said that in visits to Kuwait, Qatar and Saudi Arabia over the past week he received strong support from the Gulf Arab leaders for continued security cooperation in "dual containment" deterrence of Iraq and Iran.
"It's a dangerous neighbourhood," said Perry. "We had very strong agreement among all of us on the continuing necessity for regional security."

Saudi Arabia executed four dissident Saudis after last year's bombing. The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation and Saudi authorities are still investigating the second incident which killed 19 American airmen at a military housing complex in Dhahran.

Earlier on Saturday, a senior defence official told reporters travelling with Perry that King Fahd and the secretary noted during their meeting that a joint U.S.-Saudi investigation on the June bombing had "reached no conclusion yet and was still continuing".

During visits to Prince Sultan airbase and Eskan village on Saturday, Perry praised U.S. troops, calling their mission one of the most important international military obligations of the United States in an area which sits on three-quarters of the world's oil reserves.
"You are here to prevent war," he told airmen at Sultan, where nearly 80 U.S., British and French warplanes are taking part in policing a no-fly zone over southern Iraq.
"It says to Iraq, it says to Iran: 'Don't even think about messing with these countries'," he added, referring to U.S. allies in the Gulf.

Eskan village, originally built by the Saudis for bedouins, has about 800 air conditioned villas surrounded by a 12-foot (3.5-metre) -high wall topped by barbed wire and a 400-foot (120-metre) "exclusion zone" between the highway and the outer perimeter.
Three checkpoints guarded by soldiers with automatic weapons and guard dogs control access.
